title: Isaiah 3 — Jerusalem's leaders judged and the daughters of Zion stripped of their finery

verdicts.reasoning: Re-parsed MT: ha-adon YHWH tseva'ot meisir ... mash'en u-mash'enah (m. + f. of one noun; f. hapax), 'support and staff' standard. The line is accurate; the open question is the project-level divine-title convention for ha-adon vs adonai (escalated by the Editor), which needs a founder ruling across 1:24; 3:1; 10:16, 33; 19:4. The site list was checked: WLC (Sefaria, 'Tanach with Ta'amei Hamikra') reads ha-adon YHWH tseva'ot at 10:16 as well. Reviewer note for the ruling: option B 'the Sovereign' has strong modern precedent (NRSV, NJPS) and fits the house style of distinguishing divine titles; option A is also defensible.
Re-parsed: gibbor, ish milchamah, shofet, navi, qosem, zaqen, each rendered by its standard equivalent. No note needed. Dropping the Genesis-scoped navi entry is correct.

citations: 2 Kgs 5:1; Isa 9:14 (MT numbering) for nesu panim
verdicts.reasoning: Disputed: MT charashim (pl. of charash 'craftsman') against the homonym 'magic' (RSV/NRSV 'skilful magician'). The line follows MT vowels and the commentary reports the alternative fairly. 'The man of rank' for nesu panim and 'the skilled enchanter' for nevon lachash are standard. The cross-references (Jer 8:17; Eccl 10:11; Ps 58:6 MT) check out.

'Boys ... babes' follows the parallelism (NRSV, KJV). The abstract 'caprice' reading from 66:4 is correctly reported. In the line, 'children' for ne'arim is acceptable, though the note's gloss is 'boys'.
Re-parsed: Niphal ngs 'be oppressed', yirhavu 'act insolently', ha-niqleh / ha-nikbad 'despised / honored'. Standard; no lens.

Temporal ki opens a protasis completed in 3:7. 'Saying' is supplied for the asyndetic direct speech, which is standard practice. Ha-makshelah ha-zot 'this ruin' is standard (NRSV 'heap of ruins'). No lens.

citations: NJPS 'shall swear' (oath reading) vs NRSV 'will cry out'
verdicts.reasoning: Yissa without an object: 'lift up his voice' is the usual supplement (cf. 42:2, 11), and the oath reading is reported. Chovesh 'healer' (chbsh of binding wounds, 1:6; 30:26; 61:1) is standard.

citations: BDB s.v. 'ayin; s.v. marah (Hiphil inf. lamrot)
verdicts.reasoning: Re-parsed: lamrot is a syncopated Hiphil infinitive of mrh. The note's claim that the consonants spell eney defectively matches the source. The literal 'eyes of his glory' is a defensible, non-lens rendering, and the presence sense is kept to commentary.

citations: NJPS 3:9 'Their partiality in judgment accuses them'
verdicts.reasoning: Hakkarat (hapax) 'the look of their faces' (NRSV) is kept, and the forensic 'partiality' reading (NJPS; Deut 1:17; 16:19) is accurately reported. 'Woe to their soul' follows book precedent.

citations: Old Greek Isa 3:10: dēsōmen ton dikaion hoti dyschrēstos hēmin estin (cf. Wis 2:12)
verdicts.reasoning: MT imru tsaddiq ki-tov is kept and the conjectural ashrey is reported as unsupported, which matches the MT policy. The Old Greek claim ('Let us bind the righteous, for he is troublesome to us') is accurate.
Oy le-rasha ra' (atnach on ra'): 'Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him' matches the accents. Gemul yadav 'what his hands have dealt out' is standard.

citations: Old Greek Isa 3:12: praktores hymōn kalamōntai hymas, kai hoi apaitountes kyrieuousin hymōn
BDB s.v. 'alal II 'act the child' (Po. ptc. Isa 3:12) vs 'alal I 'deal severely, glean' (Lam 1:22; 2:20)
verdicts.reasoning: The line is approved: MT nashim 'women', 'children', 'destroyed', with the Old Greek 'glean' and 'exactors/creditors' correctly reported. The commentary needs a precision fix. The 'glean' reading needs no different vowels, because MT me'olel is a Poel participle that can belong to either homonym. Proposed wording: 'The same form can instead be derived from the homonym 'll "deal severely, glean" (Lam 1:22; 2:20): "their oppressors glean them", which is the sense of the Old Greek.' Add that me'olel is singular, rendered as a collective. Make the same fix in lexical-cruxes-isaiah-3 ('Masoretic vocalisation' becomes 'Masoretic reading').

citations: Old Greek Isa 3:13 ton laon autou; Peshitta 'his people' (both cited in the NRSV footnote 'Gk Syr')
verdicts.reasoning: The MT 'ammim is kept and the Old Greek + Syriac 'his people' is accurately reported. The note's harmonising remark is fair and makes no lens claim.
Bi'artem 'you have eaten up' (NRSV 'devoured') follows the grazing sense, which the vineyard image and 5:5 support. The 6:13 contrast is noted, and 6:13 itself is disputed elsewhere.

The line is approved: the qere mah-lakhem is translated, and the compound formula is rendered correctly. The commentary contains a factual error. The one-word consonants mlkm cannot mean 'your king' (that would be malkekhem, mlkkm). They read malkam 'their king', or the divine name Milcom. Proposed wording: 'Read as one word, the consonants could be taken as malkām "their king", but that is not the received reading.'

The qere netuyot is translated correctly. The hapaxes are handled in the conventional way: mesaqqerot 'wanton eyes' (KJV/NRSV tradition) with 'painting the eyes' reported, tafof 'mincing', and te'akkasnah as a denominative from 'ekhes, 'jingling'. No lens.

citations: BDB s.v. saphach (Piel 'smite with scab'); s.v. pot
verdicts.reasoning: 'Strike with scabs' and 'secret parts' are the standard renderings (NRSV). The Old Greek 'will humble' and the Akkadian pūtu 'forehead' alternative are accurately reported. Adonai and YHWH are kept distinct, as in the source.

'Anklets / headbands / crescents' are conventional (NRSV 'headbands, crescents'), and the count of twenty-one items is correct. The 'little suns' etymology is the standard etymological suggestion; Reviewer did not separately check it against HALOT. It and the protective-lunar reading are confined to commentary and labelled as interpretation. Lens check passes.
'Pendants, bracelets, scarves' are conventional modern renderings (NRSV 'pendants, bracelets, scarfs'). Keeping 'veils' for redidim is a sound one-word-one-English discipline.

The renderings are standard, and the cross-references check out (Exod 39:28; 61:10; 2 Sam 1:10; Jer 2:32). The 'amulet cases' alternative for batey ha-nefesh is in commentary only. Reading lechashim as amulets is lexical, not a lens choice.
Tabba'ot 'rings', nizmey ha-af 'nose rings' (Gen 24:47): standard.
The renderings are standard, and the references are accurate (Zech 3:4; Ruth 3:15; 2 Kgs 5:23).

citations: Vulgate Isa 3:23 'et specula et sindones et vittas et theristra'
Old Greek Isa 3:23 ta diaphanē Lakōnika
verdicts.reasoning: 'Hand mirrors' (Vulgate specula, cf. gillayon 8:1) against 'garments of gauze' (Old Greek 'transparent Laconian [garments]'): both are defensible, and both version claims are verified. The other items are standard (Judg 14:12-13; Prov 31:24; Zech 3:5; Song 5:7).

citations: BDB s.v. kî II 'branding' (cf. kewiyyah, Exod 21:25)
verdicts.reasoning: MT ki as a noun, 'branding instead of beauty', is kept under the MT policy. The 1QIsaᵃ plus bwšt is reported accurately. The 'girdle' / 'girding' change is a good lexical discipline (chgr). Miqsheh 'well-set hair' follows the KJV tradition, and the hapaxes niqpah and petigil are conventional.
Fem. sg. address to Zion (metayikh, gevuratekh) is correctly observed. The abstract-for-concrete 'your mighty' is standard.

citations: BDB s.v. naqah Niphal 'be cleaned out' (Zech 5:3)
verdicts.reasoning: 'Emptied' for veniqqatah is a defensible, recognised sense (NRSV 'ravaged'), and the mourning posture (47:1) is correctly noted.

glossaryReview.reasoning: claim_type direct is correct: every option is a standard rendering. The site list is accurate (10:16 verified in WLC). The provisional wohChoice awaits the founder's book-level ruling (A 'the Lord' / B 'the Sovereign' / C 'the Master'), which must be applied at all five sites and merged with the chapter-1 entry.
Strong's H3908 is correct. The context-sensitive senses (charm at 3:3, amulets at 3:20, the 26:16 prayer ruling untouched) match the lexica, and the cited verses check out. direct is correct.

The renderings, the one-word-one-English rule and the containment of astral and magical readings are all sound, and direct is correct. Two fixes are needed. (1) The source field misspells the 3:16 participle as יְשַׂקְּרוֹת; it should be מְשַׂקְּרוֹת, as in MT and in the entry's own translit. (2) The Strong's string all matches Reviewer recall (H8265, H2952, H5913, H5596, H6596, H5914, H7636, H7720, H5188, H8285, H7479, H6287, H6807, H7196, H1004+H5315, H3908, H2885, H5141+H639, H4254, H4594, H4304, H2754, H1549, H5466, H6797, H7289, H2290, H5364, H4639+H4748, H6614, H3587). Replace '(Reviewer to verify)' with '(checked from Reviewer recall 2026-11-26; not concordance-verified)', or machine-check against a Strong's concordance before stable.

The entry is otherwise approved, and direct is correct. One rationale wording should change: 'follows the Masoretic vocalisation of me'olel over the Old Greek's glean' should read 'Masoretic reading (homonym 'll II "act as a child")', because both senses fit the same vowels (see ISA-3:12). The Strong's numbers match Reviewer recall (H4937, H4938, H2450+H2796, H5375+H6440, H8586, H5375, H2280, H3782, H1971+H6440, H188+H5315, H5953, H1104, H1197, H1369, H5352). The note should change to 'checked from Reviewer recall, not concordance-verified'. H5315, H5375, H6440 and H1004 also agree with existing central-glossary entries.
The six extensions apply the existing policy correctly. Each ancient-version claim in the rationaleAppend was checked and is accurate.
The extensions to 3:1 and 3:15 match the source (צְבָאוֹת present at both).
Source reads standalone אֲדֹנָי at 3:17 and 3:18, so the extension is correct.
Source 3:15 reads אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה צְבָאוֹת, so combining the entries as 'the Lord YHWH of hosts' is correct.
3:8 has suffixed kevodo in the construct phrase 'eney kevodo, so the extension is correct and the literal rendering is kept.
The chapter title is descriptive, not lens-bearing, and the oy 'Woe' convention is consistent.
Central extension to ISA-3:24 (five tachat clauses) is correct. The rationaleAppend properly defers the ki crux to the overlay policy.

paragraphs.text: כִּי֩ הִנֵּ֨ה הָאָד֜וֹן יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֗וֹת מֵסִ֤יר מִירוּשָׁלִַ֙ם֙ וּמִ֣יהוּדָ֔ה מַשְׁעֵ֖ן וּמַשְׁעֵנָ֑ה כֹּ֚ל מִשְׁעַן־לֶ֔חֶם וְכֹ֖ל מִשְׁעַן־מָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: For behold, the Sovereign, YHWH of hosts, is taking away from Jerusalem and from Judah support and staff — all support of bread and all support of water;

notes.official:
*hā-ʾāḏôn*, the singular noun *ʾāḏôn* "lord, master" with the definite article, stands before *YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* here, as at 1:24, 10:16, 10:33 and 19:4 (cf. Exod 23:17; 34:23, *hā-ʾāḏōn YHWH*). It is a different word from the title *ʾăḏōnāy*, which the book's house style renders "the Lord" (3:17, 18; 6:1). The line renders *hā-ʾāḏôn* "the Sovereign" (NRSV, NJPS), so that the English keeps the two titles apart; ASV and KJV have "the Lord" for both (overlay `ha-adon-articular-title-isaiah`).

*mašʿēn ûmašʿēnāh* sets the masculine and feminine forms of one noun, "support", side by side; the feminine form occurs only here. The pair is a merism for every kind of support, and the verse spells it out at once: "all support of bread and all support of water." The supports then become persons: 3:2–3 names the pillars of the state one by one.

paragraphs.translit: kī hinnēh hāʾādōn YHWH ṣəbāʾōt mēsīr mīrūšālim ūmīhūdāh mašʿēn ūmašʿēnāh kōl mišʿan-leḥem wəkōl mišʿan-māyim

paragraphs.text: גִּבּ֖וֹר וְאִ֣ישׁ מִלְחָמָ֑ה שׁוֹפֵ֥ט וְנָבִ֖יא וְקֹסֵ֥ם וְזָקֵֽן׃

i18n.en: the mighty man and the man of war, the judge and the prophet, the diviner and the elder;

paragraphs.translit: gibbōr wəʾīš milḥāmāh šōpēṭ wənābīʾ wəqōsēm wəzāqēn

paragraphs.text: שַׂר־חֲמִשִּׁ֖ים וּנְשׂ֣וּא פָנִ֑ים וְיוֹעֵ֛ץ וַחֲכַ֥ם חֲרָשִׁ֖ים וּנְב֥וֹן לָֽחַשׁ׃

i18n.en: the captain of fifty and the man of rank, the counselor and the expert craftsman, and the skilled enchanter.

notes.official:
*nᵉśûʾ p̄ānîm*, literally "lifted of face", is a man of standing (2 Kgs 5:1, of Naaman; Isa 9:14). The line gives "the man of rank" rather than "the honored man" so that it stays distinct from *nikbāḏ* "the honored" in 3:5.

*ḥăḵam ḥărāšîm* is read with the Masoretic vowels as the plural of *ḥārāš* "craftsman": "the expert craftsman". Craftsmen are among the classes deported in 597 BCE (2 Kgs 24:14, 16), which suits a list of what the city will lose. Because the item stands between the diviner (3:2) and the expert in *laḥaš*, the lexica also list a homonym *ḥereš* "magic art" for this verse, and several modern translations render "skilful magician". The consonants allow that reading; it is noted here and not adopted.

*nᵉḇôn laḥaš*, "one skilled in *laḥaš*": the noun means a whisper, and in this register a whispered spell or charm (Jer 8:17; Eccl 10:11; cf. the "charmers" of Ps 58:6). Hence "the skilled enchanter". The same noun names the amulets of 3:20; at 26:16 it is a hushed prayer (`tzaqun-lachash-whispered-prayer-isaiah-26`). The list in 3:2–3 counts the diviner and the enchanter among the leaders of the state, next to the judge and the prophet, and does not comment on them.

paragraphs.translit: śar-ḥămiššīm ūnəśūʾ pānīm wəyōʿēṣ waḥăkam ḥărāšīm ūnəbōn lāḥaš

paragraphs.text: וְנָתַתִּ֥י נְעָרִ֖ים שָׂרֵיהֶ֑ם וְתַעֲלוּלִ֖ים יִמְשְׁלוּ־בָֽם׃

i18n.en: And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them.

notes.official: *taʿălûlîm* stands parallel to *nᵉʿārîm* "boys" and is rendered "babes". Its only other occurrence is 66:4, where it means "caprices" or "wanton dealings" (root *ʿll* "act wantonly"). Some interpreters therefore read it abstractly here too: "caprice shall rule over them", that is, capricious rulers. The concrete sense fits the parallelism and returns in 3:12; the abstract sense is noted.

paragraphs.translit: wənātattī nəʿārīm śārēhem wətaʿălūlīm yimšəlū-bām

paragraphs.text: וְנִגַּ֣שׂ הָעָ֔ם אִ֥ישׁ בְּאִ֖ישׁ וְאִ֣ישׁ בְּרֵעֵ֑הוּ יִרְהֲב֗וּ הַנַּ֙עַר֙ בַּזָּקֵ֔ן וְהַנִּקְלֶ֖ה בַּנִּכְבָּֽד׃

i18n.en: And the people shall be oppressed, man by man and each by his neighbor; the youth shall be insolent toward the elder, and the despised toward the honored.

paragraphs.translit: wəniggaś hāʿām ʾīš bəʾīš wəʾīš bərēʿēhū yirhăbū hannaʿar bazzāqēn wəhanniqleh bannikbād

paragraphs.text: כִּֽי־יִתְפֹּ֨שׂ אִ֤ישׁ בְּאָחִיו֙ בֵּ֣ית אָבִ֔יו שִׂמְלָ֣ה לְכָ֔ה קָצִ֖ין תִּֽהְיֶה־לָּ֑נוּ וְהַמַּכְשֵׁלָ֥ה הַזֹּ֖את תַּ֥חַת יָדֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: When a man takes hold of his brother in his father's house, saying: “You have a cloak; you shall be our ruler, and let this ruin be under your hand” —

paragraphs.translit: kī-yitpōś ʾīš bəʾāḥīw bēt ʾābīw śimlāh ləkāh qāṣīn tihyeh-lānū wəhammakšēlāh hazzōʾt taḥat yādekā

paragraphs.text: יִשָּׂא֩ בַיּ֨וֹם הַה֤וּא ׀ לֵאמֹר֙ לֹא־אֶהְיֶ֣ה חֹבֵ֔שׁ וּבְבֵיתִ֕י אֵ֥ין לֶ֖חֶם וְאֵ֣ין שִׂמְלָ֑ה לֹ֥א תְשִׂימֻ֖נִי קְצִ֥ין עָֽם׃

i18n.en: in that day he will lift up his voice, saying: “I will not be a healer; in my house there is neither bread nor cloak; you shall not make me ruler of the people.”

notes.official:
*yiśśāʾ* has no expressed object. The line supplies "his voice", the usual ellipsis with *nāśāʾ* (cf. 42:2, 11): the man protests aloud. Others understand the ellipsis as raising the hand in an oath (cf. *nāśāʾ yāḏ*), "he will swear"; the sense is close, since the refusal that follows is solemn.

*ḥōḇēš* is "one who binds up", the verb used for binding wounds (1:6; 30:26; 61:1); hence "a healer". The refusal recalls the unbandaged wounds of 1:5–6. An alternative reading, "one who binds on" the turban of office, is not adopted.

paragraphs.translit: yiśśāʾ bayyōm hahūʾ | lēʾmōr lōʾ-ʾehyeh ḥōbēš ūbəbētī ʾēn leḥem wəʾēn śimlāh lōʾ təśīmunī qəṣīn ʿām

paragraphs.text: כִּ֤י כָשְׁלָה֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וִיהוּדָ֖ה נָפָ֑ל כִּֽי־לְשׁוֹנָ֤ם וּמַֽעַלְלֵיהֶם֙ אֶל־יְהוָ֔ה לַמְר֖וֹת עֵנֵ֥י כְבוֹדֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen, because their tongue and their deeds are against YHWH, to defy the eyes of his glory.

notes.official:
*kāšᵉlāh* "has stumbled" is kept literal because it takes up *ham-makšēlāh* of 3:6, "this ruin", literally "this stumbling-heap": the heap the brother is asked to govern is the city that has stumbled.

*lamrôṯ ʿênê kᵉḇôḏô*, "to defy the eyes of his glory". The consonantal text spells *ʿênê* "the eyes of" defectively (*ʿny* for *ʿyny*), and the construct phrase is rendered literally. *kāḇôḏ* is the weighty, visible presence of YHWH (6:3; `kevodo-kavod-suffixed-isaiah`), and the phrase gives that presence eyes, before which Judah's words and deeds take place. A smoother rendering such as "his glorious presence" would lose the image.

paragraphs.translit: kī kāšəlāh yərūšālim wīhūdāh nāpāl kī-ləšōnām ūmaʿallēhem ʾel-YHWH lamrōt ʿēnē kəbōdō

paragraphs.text: הַכָּרַ֤ת פְּנֵיהֶם֙ עָ֣נְתָה בָּ֔ם וְחַטָּאתָ֛ם כִּסְדֹ֥ם הִגִּ֖ידוּ לֹ֣א כִחֵ֑דוּ א֣וֹי לְנַפְשָׁ֔ם כִּֽי־גָמְל֥וּ לָהֶ֖ם רָעָֽה׃

i18n.en: The look of their faces testifies against them; they declare their sin like Sodom, they do not hide it. Woe to their soul! For they have brought evil upon themselves.

notes.official:
*hakkāraṯ pᵉnêhem* is rendered "the look of their faces". The noun occurs only here. It can also be derived from the idiom *hikkîr pānîm*, "show partiality" in judgment (Deut 1:17; 16:19; Prov 24:23), which gives "their partiality testifies against them" and anticipates the charge against the elders and princes in 3:14–15. The line keeps the visual sense, which the parallel "they declare their sin like Sodom, they do not hide it" supports. The forensic reading is noted.

*ʾôy lᵉnap̄šām*, "Woe to their soul!", keeps the book's usual rendering "soul" for *nep̄eš* (15:4; 26:9; 29:8). Here *nep̄eš* comes close to a reflexive, "Woe to them", as the next clause ("they have brought evil upon themselves") shows. *ʾôy* is rendered "Woe", as *hôy* is throughout the book. The comparison with Sodom takes up 1:9–10.

paragraphs.translit: hakkārat pənēhem ʿānətāh bām wəḥaṭṭāʾtām kisdōm higgīdū lōʾ kiḥēdū ʾōy lənapšām kī-gāməlū lāhem rāʿāh

paragraphs.text: אִמְר֥וּ צַדִּ֖יק כִּי־ט֑וֹב כִּֽי־פְרִ֥י מַעַלְלֵיהֶ֖ם יֹאכֵֽלוּ׃

i18n.en: Say of the righteous that it shall be well with him, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.

notes.official: The line follows the Masoretic Text: *ʾimrû ṣaddîq kî-ṭôḇ*, "Say of the righteous that it shall be well". The singular *ṣaddîq* is resumed by the plural *yōʾḵēlû* "they shall eat", a collective use that the line keeps. A frequently proposed emendation reads *ʾašrê ṣaddîq*, "Happy is the righteous", which smooths the syntax and makes a beatitude to answer the "Woe" of 3:11. It has no manuscript support and is not adopted (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`). The Old Greek reads quite different words, "Let us bind the righteous, for he is troublesome to us". Verses 10–11 form a wisdom-style pair on the outcome of deeds, set inside the oracle.

paragraphs.translit: ʾimrū ṣaddīq kī-ṭōb kī-pərī maʿallēhem yōʾkēlū

paragraphs.text: א֖וֹי לְרָשָׁ֣ע רָ֑ע כִּֽי־גְמ֥וּל יָדָ֖יו יֵעָ֥שֶׂה לּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him.

paragraphs.translit: ʾōy lərāšāʿ rāʿ kī-gəmūl yādāyw yēʿāśeh lō

paragraphs.text: עַמִּי֙ נֹגְשָׂ֣יו מְעוֹלֵ֔ל וְנָשִׁ֖ים מָ֣שְׁלוּ ב֑וֹ עַמִּי֙ מְאַשְּׁרֶ֣יךָ מַתְעִ֔ים וְדֶ֥רֶךְ אֹֽרְחֹתֶ֖יךָ בִּלֵּֽעוּ׃ (ס)

i18n.en: My people — children are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, those who lead you cause you to go astray, and they have destroyed the way of your paths.

notes.official:
Two text-critical decisions and one lexical one.

*nōḡᵉśāyw mᵉʿôlēl* is read as the Poel participle of *ʿll* "act as a child" (related to *ʿôlēl* "child"): "children are their oppressors". The participle is singular and is rendered as a collective. The people's taskmasters behave like children, which takes up 3:4. The same form can instead be derived from the homonym *ʿll* "deal severely, glean" (Lam 1:22; 2:20): "their oppressors glean them", which is the sense of the Old Greek. No change of vowels is needed for either reading. *wᵉnāšîm* "and women" is the Masoretic reading. The Old Greek points to *nōšîm* "creditors", a word that pairs well with "oppressors". Both readings are reported here, and the line keeps the Masoretic Text (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

*billēʿû* is taken from *blʿ* "swallow", "they have destroyed (literally swallowed up) the way of your paths". A homonym *blʿ* "confuse" (19:3; 28:7) would match *matʿîm* "cause to go astray"; 9:15 sets the same two verbs side by side for the same leaders. The line keeps "destroyed"; "confused" is the main alternative.

paragraphs.translit: ʿammī nōgəśāyw məʿōlēl wənāšīm māšəlū bō ʿammī məʾaššərēkā matʿīm wəderek ʾōrəḥōtēkā billēʿū (s)

paragraphs.text: נִצָּ֥ב לָרִ֖יב יְהוָ֑ה וְעֹמֵ֖ד לָדִ֥ין עַמִּֽים׃

i18n.en: YHWH takes his stand to contend, and stands to judge the peoples.

notes.official: *lāḏîn ʿammîm*, "to judge the peoples", is the Masoretic reading. The Old Greek and the Syriac have "his people", which suits the case against "the elders of his people" in 3:14. The Masoretic Text is kept (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`): YHWH takes his stand as judge of the peoples and then turns to the case against his own.

paragraphs.translit: niṣṣāb lārīb YHWH wəʿōmēd lādīn ʿammīm

paragraphs.text: יְהוָה֙ בְּמִשְׁפָּ֣ט יָב֔וֹא עִם־זִקְנֵ֥י עַמּ֖וֹ וְשָׂרָ֑יו וְאַתֶּם֙ בִּֽעַרְתֶּ֣ם הַכֶּ֔רֶם גְּזֵלַ֥ת הֶֽעָנִ֖י בְּבָתֵּיכֶֽם׃

i18n.en: YHWH will enter into judgment with the elders of his people and its princes: It is you who have eaten up the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses.

notes.official: *biʿartem hak-kerem*, "you have eaten up the vineyard". Here *bʿr* is the verb used of livestock grazing a field bare (Exod 22:4), not the *bʿr* "burn" of 6:13. The vineyard is the people, as in the song of 5:1–7, where the same verb returns (5:5). *gᵉzēlaṯ he-ʿānî*, "the plunder of the poor" in their houses, is the evidence against the accused.

paragraphs.translit: YHWH bəmišpāṭ yābōʾ ʿim-ziqnē ʿammō wəśārāyw wəʾattem biʿartem hakkerem gəzēlat heʿānī bəbāttēkem

paragraphs.text: מלכם [מַה־] [לָּכֶם֙] תְּדַכְּא֣וּ עַמִּ֔י וּפְנֵ֥י עֲנִיִּ֖ים תִּטְחָ֑נוּ נְאֻם־אֲדֹנָ֥י יְהוִ֖ה צְבָאֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: What do you mean by crushing my people and grinding the face of the poor? says the Lord YHWH of hosts.

notes.official:
The consonantal text writes *mlkm* as one word (ketiv). The qere divides it as *mah-lāḵem*, "What is it to you…?", that is, "What do you mean by…?", and the line translates the qere (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`). Read as one word, the consonants could be taken as *malkām* "their king", but that is not the received reading.

The closing formula *nᵉʾum ʾăḏōnāy YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* joins the compound name *ʾăḏōnāy YHWH* ("the Lord YHWH") to *ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ* ("of hosts"). It is rendered "says the Lord YHWH of hosts" by combining the two existing name conventions, with *nᵉʾum* "says" as at 14:22–23.

paragraphs.translit: mlkm [mah] [lākem] tədakkəʾū ʿammī ūpənē ʿăniyyīm tiṭḥānū nəʾum-ʾădōnāy YHWH ṣəbāʾōt (s)

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה יַ֚עַן כִּ֤י גָֽבְהוּ֙ בְּנ֣וֹת צִיּ֔וֹן וַתֵּלַ֙כְנָה֙ נטוות [נְטוּי֣וֹת] גָּר֔וֹן וּֽמְשַׂקְּר֖וֹת עֵינָ֑יִם הָל֤וֹךְ וְטָפֹף֙ תֵּלַ֔כְנָה וּבְרַגְלֵיהֶ֖ם תְּעַכַּֽסְנָה׃

i18n.en: And YHWH said: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with outstretched necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and jingling with their feet,

notes.official:
The line reads the qere *nᵉṭûyôṯ* "outstretched" for the ketiv *nṭwwt*, an orthographic variant with the same sense (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

*mᵉśaqqᵉrôṯ ʿênāyim* (the verb occurs only here) is rendered "wanton eyes": glancing or ogling, from a root attested in Aramaic for "look at". Some take it instead as "painting the eyes". *ṭāp̄ōp̄*, "taking small steps, mincing", is also unique. *tᵉʿakkasnāh* is a verb formed from *ʿeḵes* "anklet" (3:18): the women make their anklets sound as they walk, hence "jingling with their feet".

paragraphs.translit: wayyōʾmer YHWH yaʿan kī gābəhū bənōt ṣiyyōn wattēlaknāh nṭwwt [nəṭūyōt] gārōn ūməśaqqərōt ʿēnāyim hālōk wəṭāpōp tēlaknāh ūbəraglēhem təʿakkasnāh

paragraphs.text: וְשִׂפַּ֣ח אֲדֹנָ֔י קָדְקֹ֖ד בְּנ֣וֹת צִיּ֑וֹן וַיהוָ֖ה פָּתְהֵ֥ן יְעָרֶֽה׃ (ס)

i18n.en: the Lord will strike with scabs the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and YHWH will lay bare their secret parts.

notes.official:
*wᵉśippaḥ* is related to *sappaḥaṯ* "scab" (Lev 13:2; 14:56), hence "will strike with scabs the crown of the head". The Old Greek has "will humble". Some propose "will make bald", which 3:24 ("instead of well-set hair, baldness") would support.

*pāṯhēn yᵉʿāreh*. *pōṯ* means "socket, opening" at 1 Kgs 7:50, hence the traditional "their secret parts": the public stripping of captive women (47:2–3; Nah 3:5). The Akkadian word *pūtu* "forehead" suggests "will lay bare their foreheads" instead, in parallel with *qoḏqōḏ* "crown of the head". That reading is noted, and the traditional sense is kept. The verse alternates *ʾăḏōnāy* "the Lord" and *YHWH*, and the line keeps the two distinct.

paragraphs.translit: wəśippaḥ ʾădōnāy qādəqōd bənōt ṣiyyōn waYHWH pātəhēn yəʿāreh (s)

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֨וֹם הַה֜וּא יָסִ֣יר אֲדֹנָ֗י אֵ֣ת תִּפְאֶ֧רֶת הָעֲכָסִ֛ים וְהַשְּׁבִיסִ֖ים וְהַשַּׂהֲרֹנִֽים׃

i18n.en: In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, and the headbands, and the crescents;

notes.official:
The catalogue in 3:18–23 lists twenty-one items. Several occur nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, and the identification of many is uncertain (Wildberger, *Isaiah 1–12*; Williamson, ICC *Isaiah 1–5*, 2006). The translation gives a conventional rendering for each item and a different English word for each Hebrew word. These notes record where the identification is open (`daughters-of-zion-finery-isaiah-3`).

*tip̄ʾereṯ hā-ʿăḵāsîm*, "the finery of the anklets" (*ʿeḵes*, cf. Prov 7:22), is fairly secure. *šᵉḇîsîm* (only here) is rendered "headbands". In later Hebrew *šᵉḇîs* is a hair-net or headband; older English has "cauls". A derivation from a word for "sun" (cf. Arabic *šumaisa* "little sun") would make them sun-shaped discs, paired with the crescents that follow. That identification is uncertain and is not adopted.

*śahărōnîm*, "crescents", are moon-shaped ornaments, worn also by the camels of the Midianite kings (Judg 8:21, 26). Crescent pendants are common in the jewellery of the ancient Near East, and many interpreters take them as lunar emblems worn for protection. That is an interpretive reading of the ornament's function (inferred, not stated in the text), and the line does not carry it.

paragraphs.translit: bayyōm hahūʾ yāsīr ʾădōnāy ʾēt tipʾeret hāʿăkāsīm wəhaššəbīsīm wəhaśśahărōnīm

paragraphs.text: הַנְּטִיפ֥וֹת וְהַשֵּׁיר֖וֹת וְהָֽרְעָלֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: the pendants, and the bracelets, and the scarves;

notes.official: *nᵉṭîp̄ôṯ*, "pendants" (literally "drops", from *nṭp* "drip"), appear with the crescents at Judg 8:26. *šêrôṯ* (only here), "bracelets", matches a word for bracelet or chain in Aramaic; "chains" is possible. *rᵉʿālôṯ* (only here) is rendered "scarves". An Arabic word for a long veil suggests some kind of veil or head-covering, but "veils" is reserved for *rᵉḏîḏîm* (3:23) so that each Hebrew word has its own English.

paragraphs.translit: hannəṭīpōt wəhaššērōt wəhārəʿālōt

paragraphs.text: הַפְּאֵרִ֤ים וְהַצְּעָדוֹת֙ וְהַקִּשֻּׁרִ֔ים וּבָתֵּ֥י הַנֶּ֖פֶשׁ וְהַלְּחָשִֽׁים׃

i18n.en: the headdresses, and the ankle chains, and the sashes, and the perfume boxes, and the amulets;

notes.official:
*pᵉʾērîm*, "headdresses": the word is used of the priests' headgear (Exod 39:28) and the bridegroom's headdress (61:10). *ṣᵉʿāḏôṯ*, "ankle chains", from *ṣʿd* "step"; the related *ʾeṣʿāḏāh* is an armlet (2 Sam 1:10), so "armlets" is also possible. *qiššurîm*, "sashes" (from *qšr* "tie"), are part of a bride's attire at Jer 2:32.

*bāttê han-nep̄eš*, literally "houses of the *nep̄eš*", is rendered "perfume boxes", taking *nep̄eš* in its sense of breath or scent. Another view takes them as amulet cases, small containers worn to protect the wearer's life (*nep̄eš*), which would group them with the next item. The book's usual rendering of *nep̄eš*, "soul" (3:9), is not used in this name for an object.

*lᵉḥāšîm*, "amulets": objects that carry or embody a *laḥaš*, a whispered charm (3:3; `lachash-charm-amulet-isaiah`).

paragraphs.translit: happəʾērīm wəhaṣṣəʿādōt wəhaqqiššurīm ūbāttē hannepeš wəhalləḥāšīm

paragraphs.text: הַטַּבָּע֖וֹת וְנִזְמֵ֥י הָאָֽף׃

i18n.en: the rings, and the nose rings;

notes.official: *ṭabbāʿôṯ* are signet or finger rings; *nizmê hā-ʾap̄*, "nose rings", are the rings of Gen 24:47.

paragraphs.translit: haṭṭabbāʿōt wənizmē hāʾāp

paragraphs.text: הַמַּֽחֲלָצוֹת֙ וְהַמַּ֣עֲטָפ֔וֹת וְהַמִּטְפָּח֖וֹת וְהָחֲרִיטִֽים׃

i18n.en: the festal robes, and the mantles, and the shawls, and the purses;

notes.official: *maḥălāṣôṯ*, "festal robes" (Zech 3:4), are garments put on for special occasions. *maʿăṭāp̄ôṯ* (only here, from *ʿṭp* "wrap") are "mantles". *miṭpāḥôṯ*, "shawls", is the word for the garment in Ruth 3:15, large enough to carry six measures of barley. *ḥărîṭîm*, "purses", are the bags of 2 Kgs 5:23.

paragraphs.translit: hammaḥălāṣōt wəhammaʿăṭāpōt wəhammiṭpāḥōt wəhāḥărīṭīm

paragraphs.text: וְהַגִּלְיֹנִים֙ וְהַסְּדִינִ֔ים וְהַצְּנִיפ֖וֹת וְהָרְדִידִֽים׃

i18n.en: the hand mirrors, and the fine linen garments, and the turbans, and the veils.

notes.official: *gilyōnîm* is one of the least certain items. The line follows the reading "hand mirrors", polished surfaces (cf. *gillāyôn* "tablet", 8:1), the sense the Vulgate gives. The Old Greek has transparent garments, and many modern interpreters prefer "garments of gauze", because the surrounding items in 3:22–23 are textiles. *sᵉḏînîm* are "fine linen garments" (Judg 14:12–13; Prov 31:24). *ṣᵉnîp̄ôṯ* are "turbans" (62:3; Zech 3:5). *rᵉḏîḏîm* are "veils", a light outer wrap (Song 5:7).

paragraphs.translit: wəhaggilyōnīm wəhassədīnīm wəhaṣṣənīpōt wəhārədīdīm

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָה֩ תַ֨חַת בֹּ֜שֶׂם מַ֣ק יִֽהְיֶ֗ה וְתַ֨חַת חֲגוֹרָ֤ה נִקְפָּה֙ וְתַ֨חַת מַעֲשֶׂ֤ה מִקְשֶׁה֙ קָרְחָ֔ה וְתַ֥חַת פְּתִיגִ֖יל מַחֲגֹ֣רֶת שָׂ֑ק כִּי־תַ֖חַת יֹֽפִי׃

i18n.en: And it shall be that instead of perfume there shall be rottenness; and instead of a girdle, a rope; and instead of well-set hair, baldness; and instead of a robe, a girding of sackcloth; branding instead of beauty.

notes.official:
Five *taḥaṯ* ("instead of") clauses reverse the catalogue (`tachat-substitution-formula`). *ḥăḡôrāh* is rendered "girdle", not "sash", so that its root (*ḥgr* "gird") stays audible in *maḥăḡōreṯ śaq*, "a girding of sackcloth", and so that it stays distinct from the *qiššurîm* "sashes" of 3:20. *nip̄qāh* (only here) is "a rope". *maʿăśeh miqšeh*, "well-set hair", is literally "turned (or hammered) work" (*miqšāh*, Exod 25:18), used of skilfully dressed hair. *pᵉṯîḡîl* (only here) is "a robe", a fine garment of uncertain kind.

The last clause is a textual crux. The Masoretic Text reads *kî-taḥaṯ yōp̄î* and takes *kî* as a noun, "burn-mark, branding", from *kwh* "burn" (cf. *kᵉwiyyāh*, Exod 21:25): "branding instead of beauty", perhaps the mark put on captives. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) adds *bwšt* "shame", which makes *kî* the conjunction: "for instead of beauty, shame". The line keeps the Masoretic Text (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`) and reports the Qumran reading here.

paragraphs.translit: wəhāyāh taḥat bōśem maq yihyeh wətaḥat ḥăgōrāh niqpāh wətaḥat maʿăśeh miqšeh qārəḥāh wətaḥat pətīgīl maḥăgōret śāq kī-taḥat yōpī

paragraphs.text: מְתַ֖יִךְ בַּחֶ֣רֶב יִפֹּ֑לוּ וּגְבוּרָתֵ֖ךְ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה׃

i18n.en: Your men shall fall by the sword, and your mighty in battle.

notes.official: *mᵉṯayiḵ* and *gᵉḇûrāṯēḵ* turn to address Zion in the feminine singular. *gᵉḇûrāh* is the abstract "might", used here for the city's fighting men, hence "your mighty in battle".

paragraphs.translit: mətayik baḥereb yippōlū ūgəbūrātēk bammilḥāmāh

paragraphs.text: וְאָנ֥וּ וְאָבְל֖וּ פְּתָחֶ֑יהָ וְנִקָּ֖תָה לָאָ֥רֶץ תֵּשֵֽׁב׃

i18n.en: And her gates shall lament and mourn, and, emptied, she shall sit upon the ground.

notes.official: *pᵉṯāḥêhā*, "her gates" (literally "openings"), lament. *wᵉniqqāṯāh* is the Niphal of *nqh*, which usually means "be free of guilt, go unpunished". Here, as at Zech 5:3, it means "be cleaned out, emptied": "emptied, she shall sit upon the ground", the posture of mourning (cf. 47:1).

paragraphs.translit: wəʾānū wəʾābəlū pətāḥēhā wəniqqātāh lāʾāreṣ tēšēb
